14:T1022,## Summary

Two independent Telegraf consumers run against the same bot token concurrently:

1. **`@elizaos/plugin-telegram`** — auto-enabled when `connectors.telegram.enabled === true`. Spawns its own Telegraf instance and starts long-polling.
2. **milady's standalone wrapper** at `packages/app-core/src/runtime/eliza.ts:534` (function `ensureTelegramBotPolling`) — spawns a *second* Telegraf instance with the same token, calls `bot.startPolling()`.

Telegram's `getUpdates` long-poll API delivers each update to **exactly one consumer**. Whichever long-poll wins the race for a given message gets it; the other sees nothing. Updates routed to the upstream plugin go through elizaOS message handling — which on milady is not wired to a Telegram-channel-aware agent — and silently drop. Updates routed to milady's wrapper go through `useModel` directly and reply correctly.

End result: **every other Telegram message (roughly) gets dropped silently**. From the user's perspective, the bot replies sometimes, ignores others.

## Why both exist

The wrapper was added with this comment (`packages/app-core/src/runtime/eliza.ts:531-533`):

> *"Ensure Telegram bot is polling. The upstream plugin's `bot.launch()` is not awaited and silently fails on bun/Windows. We create a standalone Telegraf instance with proper lifecycle management."*

So milady spawns its own Telegraf to work around #7241 (Bun + Telegraf 4.16.3 `launch()` readonly-property bug). But it never disables the upstream plugin to avoid the duplicate poller.

## Symptoms

- Inconsistent: bot replies to ~50% of messages, ignores the rest.
- Logs show `[milady] Telegram bot polling started` AND `[PLUGIN:TELEGRAM] Starting Telegram bot` on boot.
- `curl https://api.telegram.org/bot<token>/getUpdates` returns empty (something *did* consume them) but no `[milady] Telegram message from @user: ...` log entry for the dropped messages.

## Reproduction

1. Fresh milady, telegram connector enabled with a valid bot token.
2. `bun run dev` — both pollers start.
3. From a Telegram client, DM the bot 5 messages back to back.
4. ~2-3 will get a reply, ~2-3 will be silently dropped depending on which poller wins each `getUpdates` race.

## Workaround (verified locally)

Disable the upstream plugin so milady's wrapper is the only consumer:

```json
// ~/.milady/milady.json
{
  "plugins": {
    "entries": {
      "@elizaos/plugin-telegram": { "enabled": false },
      "telegram": { "enabled": false }
    }
  },
  "connectors": {
    "telegram": { "enabled": false /* still want the bot active */ }
  }
}
```

After restart: only one Telegraf polls, every inbound message routes through milady's wrapper, every message gets a reply. Verified with 4 back-to-back messages — 4 logged inbound, 4 logged replies.

## Suggested fix

Two paths:

1. **Mutually exclusive at config time.** When milady spawns its own wrapper (`ensureTelegramBotPolling`), it should also force-disable the upstream `@elizaos/plugin-telegram` and the `connectors.telegram` auto-enable. One owner per bot token, no exceptions.

2. **Remove the wrapper, fix the upstream plugin.** Address the `launch()` Bun bug at the source (#7241). Then the wrapper becomes unnecessary and `@elizaos/plugin-telegram` is the single source of truth.

Option 2 is the cleaner architectural fix. Option 1 is the right tactical fix until the upstream Bun issue is resolved. Either way, the current "both run, hope for the best" state is not OK because **silent message loss looks like working software** to the user.

## Why this matters

Combined with #7240 (token bridge bug) and #7241 (Telegraf launch bug), the Telegram setup path is currently unable to deliver "I sent 5 messages and got 5 replies" reliably out of the box. Even with the user's token correctly bridged into the env and the launch bug worked around, the dual-poller race means inconsistent delivery — a user-facing failure mode that's nearly impossible to diagnose without log access.

## Environment

- bun 1.3.13
- telegraf 4.16.3
- @elizaos/plugin-telegram (current alice submodule pin)
- milady on `alice` (PR #105 sync)15:Te5d,## Summary

`packages/app-core/src/api/` has **two** `export class MiladyClient` declarations:

- `client-base.ts:36` — the one all 7 augmenter files import (`client-agent`, `client-skills`, `client-chat`, `client-cloud`, `client-vincent`, `client-wallet`, `client-browser-workspace`)
- `client.ts:2277` — the one the live `client` instance is built from (`export const client = new MiladyClient()` at `client.ts:6504`)

Each augmenter does `MiladyClient.prototype.X = ...` to attach domain methods (e.g. `listAppRuns`, `listCodingAgentTaskThreads`, `sendMessage`, ~155 methods total). Because they import from `client-base.ts` and the instance is built from `client.ts`'s class, **none of those 155 methods land on the live instance**.

## Symptoms

- UI throws `client.listCodingAgentTaskThreads is not a function`, `client.listAppRuns is not a function`, etc. on every page that uses these methods.
- Errors bubble through React error boundary → chat surface freezes → text input becomes unresponsive (it's `disabled` because the surrounding state crashed).
- 343 methods present on prototype (the inline `client.ts` ones) — but the augmenter set is missing entirely.

## Reproduction

1. Fresh milady (alice, post-PR#105 sync), `bun run dev`.
2. Open dashboard → Chat or Apps tab.
3. Browser console:
   ```js
   const m = await import('/@fs/Users/.../packages/app-core/src/api/index.ts');
   ({
     listAppRuns: typeof m.client.listAppRuns,             // 'undefined' ❌
     listCodingAgentTaskThreads: typeof m.client.listCodingAgentTaskThreads, // 'undefined' ❌
     methodCount: Object.getOwnPropertyNames(Object.getPrototypeOf(m.client)).length, // 343
   })
   ```
4. UI bubbles `is not a function` errors.

## Root cause / context

`client-base.ts` was originally introduced (per its own header comment):

> *"Separated from client.ts so domain augmentation files can import the class without circular dependency issues."*

At some point during the alice merge, `client.ts` had its own `export class MiladyClient` added inline (likely a refactor that consolidated methods back into one file) — but `client-base.ts` was left in place. The 7 augmenters still target `client-base.ts`. Two separate classes, two separate prototypes. The augmenters silently augment the wrong one.

There's no compile-time error because both files export a class with the same name and same shape. TypeScript happily lets `MiladyClient.prototype.X = ...` succeed on either.

## Fix (verified locally)

Replace `client-base.ts` body with a one-line re-export shim:

```ts
export { MiladyClient } from "./client";
```

Verified locally: method count goes 343 → 500 (157 augmenter methods now land on the live instance). All `is not a function` errors disappear. Chat hydrates cleanly.

## Side-effect imports also needed

`packages/app-core/src/api/index.ts` was also missing side-effect imports for the augmenter files. Even with the re-export shim, the augmenters need to be **loaded** for their `MiladyClient.prototype.X = ...` statements to execute:

```ts
export * from "./client";

// Side-effect imports: each augments MiladyClient.prototype with methods.
import "./client-agent";
import "./client-browser-workspace";
import "./client-chat";
import "./client-cloud";
import "./client-skills";
import "./client-vincent";
import "./client-wallet";
```

These were dropped in the alice merge as well — possibly because they appear redundant after `export * from "./client"`, but they're not (imports of side-effect-only modules need explicit `import "..."` statements).

- milady on `alice` (PR #105 sync)
- React 19 + Vite dev server16:T105f,## Summary

`packages/agent/src/auth/credentials.ts:210-225` — `hasCodexCliSubscriptionAuth()` only matches the **legacy** `~/.codex/auth.json` layout:

```ts
const data = JSON.parse(fs.readFileSync(authPath, "utf-8")) as {
  auth_mode?: string;
  OPENAI_API_KEY?: string;
};
return Boolean(
  data.OPENAI_API_KEY?.trim() &&
    data.auth_mode?.trim() &&
    data.auth_mode.trim().toLowerCase() !== "api-key",
);
```

Modern `codex-cli` (≥ 0.93.0) writes a different shape — no top-level `OPENAI_API_KEY`, no `auth_mode`, just a `tokens` object:

```json
{
  "tokens": {
    "id_token": "eyJhbGciOiJSUzI1NiIs...",
    "access_token": "eyJhbGciOiJSUzI1NiIs...",
    "refresh_token": "...",
    "account_id": "..."
  },
  "last_refresh": "..."
}
```

Detection returns `false` → milady reports the user's Codex subscription as "install required" on the Settings → Connectors panel and the auto-enable map for `@elizaos/plugin-openai` is skipped. The `subscriptionProvider` resolution silently falls through, so chat routes to whatever else is configured (or fails).

## Symptoms

- User has a valid `codex login` session (verifiable: `codex --version` works, `~/.codex/auth.json` exists with `tokens` block, manual API calls with `tokens.access_token` succeed).
- Milady dashboard shows **Codex: install required** even though the CLI is installed and authenticated.
- Boot log lacks `Auto-enabled plugin: @elizaos/plugin-openai (subscription: openai-codex)`.
- Chat falls back to "Sorry, I'm having a provider issue" because routing thinks no provider is available.

## Reproduction

1. `brew install codex-cli` (or already installed — version ≥ 0.93.0)
2. `codex login` — authenticates and writes `~/.codex/auth.json` in the new format
3. `cat ~/.codex/auth.json | python3 -c "import json,sys; d=json.load(sys.stdin); print({'OPENAI_API_KEY': d.get('OPENAI_API_KEY'), 'auth_mode': d.get('auth_mode'), 'has_tokens': bool(d.get('tokens'))})"` →
   ```
   {'OPENAI_API_KEY': None, 'auth_mode': None, 'has_tokens': True}
   ```
4. Boot milady → log shows no Codex auto-enable.
5. Settings → Connectors → Codex shows "install required".

## Workaround (verified locally)

Manually translate `~/.codex/auth.json` into the milady-side `~/.eliza/auth/openai-codex.json` shape:

```python
record = {
    'id': 'default',
    'providerId': 'openai-codex',
    'label': 'Codex CLI',
    'source': 'codex-cli',
    'credentials': {
        'access': tokens['access_token'],
        'refresh': tokens['refresh_token'],
        'expires': now_ms + 3600 * 1000,
    },
    'createdAt': now_ms,
    'updatedAt': now_ms,
}
```

After writing this file + restart, milady detects the subscription and `@elizaos/plugin-openai` auto-enables.

## Suggested fix

Update `hasCodexCliSubscriptionAuth()` to recognize **both** shapes:

```ts
function hasCodexCliSubscriptionAuth(): boolean {
  const authPath = path.join(os.homedir(), ".codex", "auth.json");
  try {
    const data = JSON.parse(fs.readFileSync(authPath, "utf-8")) as {
      auth_mode?: string;
      OPENAI_API_KEY?: string;
      tokens?: {
        access_token?: string;
        refresh_token?: string;
      };
    };

    // Modern codex-cli (>= 0.93.0): tokens block present.
    if (data.tokens?.access_token?.trim()) return true;

    // Legacy: OPENAI_API_KEY + non-"api-key" auth_mode.
    return Boolean(
      data.OPENAI_API_KEY?.trim() &&
        data.auth_mode?.trim() &&
        data.auth_mode.trim().toLowerCase() !== "api-key",
    );
  } catch {
    return false;
  }
}
```

Then update the credential-import path (`importCodexCliCredentials` or wherever it lives) to translate `tokens.access_token`/`tokens.refresh_token` → `OAuthCredentials.{access,refresh,expires}` when the legacy fields are absent.

## Why it matters

Every user on a fresh install with a current `codex-cli` will hit this. The codex CLI changed its auth file format and milady's detection didn't get updated. From the user's perspective: "I logged in with codex, milady says I didn't" → confusion.

## Environment
- bun 1.3.13
- codex-cli 0.93.0 (the one written by the modern CLI)
- macOS arm64
- milady on `alice` (PR #105 sync)17:Tef5,## Summary

`@elizaos/plugin-telegram`'s startup wrapper calls `bot.launch({...})` on a `Telegraf` instance (Telegraf 4.16.3). Under Bun 1.3.13 this rejects with:

```
[milady] Telegram bot launch error: Attempted to assign to readonly property.
```

The bot never starts polling. From the user side, the bot looks alive on Telegram (Telegram's `getUpdates` queues messages waiting for it) but the runtime never receives them. No replies. UI may report "Connected" because the token is valid; the actual long-poll never started.

## Root cause

`telegraf@4.16.3/lib/telegraf.js:189` (compiled output of nullish-coalescing-assignment):

```js
async launch(config = {}, onLaunch) {
    var _a, _b;
    ...
    debug('Connecting to Telegram');
    (_a = this.botInfo) !== null && _a !== void 0 ? _a : (this.botInfo = await this.telegram.getMe());
    ...
}
```

The expression assigns to `this.botInfo`. Under Bun's CJS interop the Telegraf prototype/instance ends up with a non-writable descriptor on certain inherited fields, and the assignment trips a strict-mode `TypeError: Attempted to assign to readonly property`. Same code paths work under Node.

## Reproduction

1. Fresh milady (alice or develop), Telegram connector enabled with a valid BotFather token (in `env.TELEGRAM_BOT_TOKEN` per #7240).
2. `bun run dev`
3. Boot log:
   ```
   [PLUGIN:TELEGRAM] Starting Telegram bot
   [milady] Telegram bot polling started
   [Warn] [milady] Telegram bot launch error: Attempted to assign to readonly property.
   ```
4. DM the bot from Telegram — no inbound message appears in logs.
5. `curl https://api.telegram.org/bot<token>/getUpdates` shows the messages queued, confirming the bot itself is reachable but its long-poll never started.

## Workaround (verified locally)

In `eliza/packages/app-core/src/runtime/eliza.ts` (or wherever the wrapper is), bypass `bot.launch()` and start polling directly:

```ts
(async () => {
  try {
    await bot.telegram.deleteWebhook({ drop_pending_updates: true });
  } catch (err) {
    logger.warn(`[milady] Telegram deleteWebhook failed: ${...}`);
  }
  try {
    // @ts-expect-error - startPolling is intentionally public for this fallback
    bot.startPolling(["message", "message_reaction"]);
  } catch (err) {
    logger.warn(`[milady] Telegram startPolling failed: ${...}`);
  }
})();
```

This skips the `(this.botInfo ??= ...)` assignment that triggers the Bun strict-mode reject. Same behavior as `launch()` (long-poll mode, no webhook), without the error. Verified inbound messages reach the runtime and replies go back.

## Suggested upstream fix

Two options for the plugin layer:

1. **Wrap `bot.launch()` to use the explicit polling path on Bun:**
   ```ts
   const isBun = typeof process !== "undefined" && Boolean((process as any).versions?.bun);
   if (isBun) {
     await bot.telegram.deleteWebhook({ drop_pending_updates: true });
     bot.startPolling(["message", "message_reaction"]);
   } else {
     await bot.launch({ dropPendingUpdates: true, allowedUpdates: ["message", "message_reaction"] });
   }
   ```

2. **Pin/upgrade Telegraf** — the issue may be fixed in a newer release with a different compiled output. Worth testing against the latest 4.x and 5.x previews.

Option 1 is the safer immediate fix; option 2 is the right long-term move.

## Why this matters

This silently breaks every Bun-hosted milady install with a Telegram connector. The auto-enable log says the plugin is loaded, the dashboard says "connected", but no messages ever flow. Users have no way to diagnose this without log access, and the failure mode (warning, not error; "polling started" log fires before the launch reject because launch() is fire-and-forget) hides the bug effectively.

## Environment

- bun 1.3.13
- telegraf 4.16.3
- macOS arm64
- milady on `alice` (PR #105)18:Tf86,## Summary

The dashboard's Telegram setup writes the bot token to `connectors.telegram.botToken` in milady.json, but `@elizaos/plugin-telegram` reads it via `runtime.getSetting(\"TELEGRAM_BOT_TOKEN\")`. **No code bridges between them.** The `/api/telegram-setup/status` endpoint reports `connected: true, hasToken: true` based on the connector config, while the plugin silently starts in degraded mode with `[PLUGIN:TELEGRAM] Bot token not provided, Telegram functionality unavailable`.

This is a classic UI/runtime contract drift: setup-status looks at one source of truth (`connectors.telegram.botToken`), the plugin looks at another (`runtime.getSetting(\"TELEGRAM_BOT_TOKEN\")`), and nothing tells the user that pasting the token in the UI didn't actually wire up the bot.

## Symptoms

After completing the Settings → Connectors → Telegram setup form with a valid BotFather token:

- UI: "Telegram — Connected" (green checkmark)
- `GET /api/telegram-setup/status`: `{ available: true, hasToken: true, connected: true }`
- Backend log on boot:
  ```
  [Warn] [PLUGIN:TELEGRAM] Bot token not provided, Telegram functionality unavailable
  [Warn] [PLUGIN:TELEGRAM] Service started without bot functionality
  ```
- DMing the bot on Telegram: bot is unresponsive (it's not polling because no token reached the plugin)

## Reproduction

1. Fresh milady (alice or develop), start dev.
2. Settings → Connectors → Telegram → paste BotFather token, save.
3. Inspect `~/.milady/milady.json` — token lives at `connectors.telegram.botToken`.
4. Inspect `~/.milady/milady.json` `env` block — `TELEGRAM_BOT_TOKEN` is **not** there.
5. Boot logs show `Bot token not provided`.
6. Manually copy the token into `env.TELEGRAM_BOT_TOKEN`, restart → plugin starts polling and bot responds.

## Root cause

Two parallel config keys, no synchronization:

| Where | Read by |
|---|---|
| `connectors.telegram.botToken` | Dashboard, `/api/telegram-setup/status` |
| `env.TELEGRAM_BOT_TOKEN` (or process env) | `@elizaos/plugin-telegram` via `runtime.getSetting()` |

The setup-routes handler at `packages/agent/src/api/telegram-setup-routes.ts:144` checks `state.runtime?.getSetting(\"TELEGRAM_BOT_TOKEN\")` for `hasToken`. But the dashboard save handler writes to `connectors.telegram.botToken` only — it doesn't propagate into `env.TELEGRAM_BOT_TOKEN` and doesn't call `runtime.setSetting()`. So `hasToken` happens to read true via some other code path (likely a config-snapshot fallback) while the live runtime has no setting.

## Fix

Bridge the two in the save path. Either:

1. **In the dashboard save handler:** when persisting `connectors.telegram.botToken`, also write to `env.TELEGRAM_BOT_TOKEN` (so it's loaded into runtime settings on next boot) AND call `runtime.setSetting(\"TELEGRAM_BOT_TOKEN\", token)` (so the live plugin picks it up without restart).

2. **In the plugin's init:** read from both `runtime.getSetting(\"TELEGRAM_BOT_TOKEN\")` AND `runtime.character?.connectors?.telegram?.botToken` (or whatever the canonical config path is). Less clean — encodes UI config layout in plugin code.

Option 1 is right. Same fix should be applied to the other connector→env bridges that have the same problem (likely `discord`, `whatsapp`, `wechat`, etc. — worth grepping).

## Workaround

Until fixed, users can manually edit `~/.milady/milady.json` and add their token under the `env` block:

```json
{
  "env": {
    "TELEGRAM_BOT_TOKEN": "<token from BotFather>"
  }
}
```

I verified locally: after this edit + restart, plugin logs `Starting Telegram bot` / `Telegram bot polling started` and the bot responds.

## Why this is dangerous

The UI affirmatively shows "Connected" while nothing works. Users with no log access have no way to know setup silently failed. Other connectors likely have the same bug pattern — worth a sweep.

`packages/agent/src/auth/credentials.ts:210` (`hasCodexCliSubscriptionAuth`) only recognizes the **legacy** codex CLI `~/.codex/auth.json` shape:

```ts
function hasCodexCliSubscriptionAuth(): boolean {
  const authPath = path.join(os.homedir(), ".codex", "auth.json");
  try {
    const data = JSON.parse(fs.readFileSync(authPath, "utf-8")) as {
      auth_mode?: string;
      OPENAI_API_KEY?: string;
    };
    return Boolean(
      data.OPENAI_API_KEY?.trim() &&
        data.auth_mode?.trim() &&
        data.auth_mode.trim().toLowerCase() !== "api-key",
    );
  } catch {
    return false;
  }
}
```

Modern codex CLI (verified on **codex-cli 0.93.0**) writes a different shape — there's no top-level `OPENAI_API_KEY` and no `auth_mode`. Instead the OAuth state lives under a `tokens` object:

```json
{
  "OPENAI_API_KEY": null,
  "auth_mode": null,
  "tokens": {
    "id_token": "eyJhbGciOiJSUzI1NiIs…",
    "access_token": "…",
    "refresh_token": "…",
    "account_id": "…"
  },
  "last_refresh": "…"
}
```

With this shape the detector returns `false`, so:
- `subscriptionStatus` reports Codex as "install required" / "unavailable" even though the user is logged in.
- The plugin auto-enable map skips `@elizaos/plugin-openai (subscription: openai-codex)`.
- The provider switch falls back to "no subscription" routing.
- Chat replies become "Sorry, I'm having a provider issue."

## Reproduction

1. `brew install codex` (or any modern codex install — tested codex-cli 0.93.0)
2. `codex login` and complete the browser OAuth flow.
3. `cat ~/.codex/auth.json` — confirm `OPENAI_API_KEY` is `null` and `tokens.access_token` is set.
4. Boot milady → "Codex unavailable / install required".
5. Send any chat message → "Sorry, I'm having a provider issue".

## Fix

`hasCodexCliSubscriptionAuth` should accept either shape. Minimal change:

```ts
function hasCodexCliSubscriptionAuth(): boolean {
  const authPath = path.join(os.homedir(), ".codex", "auth.json");
  try {
    const data = JSON.parse(fs.readFileSync(authPath, "utf-8")) as {
      auth_mode?: string | null;
      OPENAI_API_KEY?: string | null;
      tokens?: {
        access_token?: string;
        refresh_token?: string;
      } | null;
    };

    // Modern codex (>= ~0.90): OAuth tokens live under `tokens`
    if (
      data.tokens?.access_token?.trim() &&
      data.tokens?.refresh_token?.trim()
    ) {
      return true;
    }

    // Legacy: top-level OPENAI_API_KEY + non-"api-key" auth_mode
    return Boolean(
      data.OPENAI_API_KEY?.trim() &&
        data.auth_mode?.trim() &&
        data.auth_mode.trim().toLowerCase() !== "api-key",
    );
  } catch {
    return false;
  }
}
```

The downstream credential-import path (`importCodexCliCredentials` and friends) also needs to read from `tokens.access_token` / `tokens.refresh_token` when those are present and the legacy fields are null. Currently the import path silently produces an empty `OAuthCredentials` record and the subscription appears configured-but-unusable.

I worked around this locally by hand-writing `~/.eliza/auth/openai-codex.json` from `~/.codex/auth.json`'s `tokens` block — that unblocks chat. But every fresh codex-CLI user is going to hit this until detection is fixed.

## Why this matters

Onboarding's "ChatGPT Sub" / "Use Codex" path tells users `codex login` is enough; nothing in the UI reveals the detection mismatch. Users see "install required" next to a CLI they just successfully logged into and assume their install is broken. Either fix detection or warn loudly when `~/.codex/auth.json` exists but has an unrecognized shape.

## Environment

- macOS, bun 1.3.13

- Discovered while reviving codex routing on milady alice after the openai-codex.json cache was cleared1a:T1044,## Summary

`packages/app-core/src/api/client.ts` and `packages/app-core/src/api/client-base.ts` both declare `export class MiladyClient`. The 7 domain augmentation files (`client-agent`, `client-skills`, `client-chat`, `client-cloud`, `client-vincent`, `client-wallet`, `client-browser-workspace`) all do `import { MiladyClient } from "./client-base"` and attach methods via `MiladyClient.prototype.X = …`. But the live `client` instance is created as `new MiladyClient()` from the **other** class declared inside `client.ts:2277`. So those prototype assignments hit a never-instantiated class.

Net effect: any code that calls a method defined in one of the augmenters (e.g. `client.listAppRuns`, `client.listCodingAgentTaskThreads`, `client.sendMessage`) throws `is not a function` at runtime. The symptom is React component trees crashing during render and the chat surface refusing to mount the message input.

I verified empirically:

```js
const c = (await import('@miladyai/app-core/api')).client;
typeof c.listAppRuns;                    // 'undefined'  ← BAD
typeof c.listCodingAgentTaskThreads;     // 'undefined'  ← BAD
Object.getOwnPropertyNames(Object.getPrototypeOf(c)).length;  // 343 (the inline methods from client.ts)
```

## Reproduction

1. Fresh clone of milady on `develop` or `alice`.
2. `bun install && bun run dev`, complete onboarding.
3. Open `/chat`. The dashboard surfaces error text like `client.listAppRuns is not a function` and `Failed to load task threads: client.listCodingAgentTaskThreads is not a function`. Once the agent-orchestrator widget crashes the message input also stops responding to keystrokes (React error boundary side effect).

## Diagnostic trail

- Class A: `packages/app-core/src/api/client.ts:2277` — `export class MiladyClient` (~6500-line file, contains 343 inline methods, owns `export const client = new MiladyClient()` at line 6504).
- Class B: `packages/app-core/src/api/client-base.ts:36` — `export class MiladyClient` (duplicate, ~809 lines).
- Augmenter pattern (7 files):
  ```ts
  import { MiladyClient } from "./client-base";
  MiladyClient.prototype.listAppRuns = async function () { … };
  ```
- `client-base.ts`'s only export is the duplicate `MiladyClient` — nothing else consumes the file.
- No file imports the augmenters by side effect, so even with the imports added the methods land on Class B which is never instantiated.

## Fix

Two parts, both required:

1. Replace the body of `packages/app-core/src/api/client-base.ts` with a re-export shim:
   ```ts
   export { MiladyClient } from "./client";
   ```
   Now augmenters and the `client` instance share a single class.

2. Add side-effect imports for all 7 augmenters to `packages/app-core/src/api/index.ts` so the `MiladyClient.prototype.X = …` assignments execute when consumers import `client`:
   ```ts
   export * from "./client";
   import "./client-agent";
   import "./client-browser-workspace";
   import "./client-chat";
   import "./client-cloud";
   import "./client-skills";
   import "./client-vincent";
   import "./client-wallet";
   ```

Verified locally: prototype method count goes from **343 → 500** (the 157 augmenter methods now attach correctly). All `is not a function` errors disappear. The chat input renders and accepts keystrokes again.

## Why this slipped through

The augmenters look like they're working because the imports succeed and the `MiladyClient.prototype.X = …` lines run without error — they just attach to the wrong class object. There's no compile-time check that catches "your augmentation target is the same identity as the instance's class," and TypeScript happily types `client.listAppRuns` correctly because both classes structurally share `MiladyClient` as a name. The first signal is a runtime `is not a function` deep inside React component code.

Worth considering: a small assertion at boot time (or a vitest unit test) that `MiladyClient.prototype` has every method declared in the augmenter `.d.ts` blocks. Would have caught this immediately.

- Discovered booting milady on `alice` (PR #105 sync) and `develop`1b:Ta4a,## tl;dr

The agent runtime hard-crashes (process-level segfault, not catchable JS error) on any host where `@napi-rs/keyring`'s libsecret backend can't reach a D-Bus Secret Service: **headless Linux servers, CI runners, Docker containers without a desktop session**. This blocks every self-hosted milady deployment.

## Root cause

Two separate but related issues, both triggered by `@elizaos/core` going ESM-only with top-level await:

### 1. `@napi-rs/keyring` segfaults instead of throwing on headless Linux

`packages/vault/src/master-key.ts` and `packages/confidant/src/{crypto/master-key,backends/keyring}.ts` wrap their keychain calls in `try/catch`, but on hosts without a D-Bus session the native binding aborts at the C level *before* the JS catch can fire. The crash shows up as:

```
panic(main thread): Segmentation fault at address 0x0
oh no: Bun has crashed. This indicates a bug in Bun, not your code.
```

`@elizaos/confidant` makes this worse by importing `@napi-rs/keyring` at the **top level** of two files — the native binding initializes at module-eval time, so just importing confidant from the agent runtime crashes the process before any defensive code can run.

### 2. CJS plugin bundles can't load async ESM `@elizaos/core`

10 elizaos-plugins ship a `dist/cjs/` bundle that does `require("@elizaos/core")` at the top level. That throws:

```
TypeError: require() async module "@elizaos/core" is unsupported.
use "await import()" instead.
```

`plugin-anthropic` already shipped the fix (drop CJS, ESM-only). The other 10 are stragglers. PR #5 on `plugin-pdf` ("dual build cjs / esm") was previously closed — that decision is consistent with this issue.

When the SwarmCoordinator dispatches a research/coding task, it spawns a `claude` (Claude Code CLI) subprocess in a PTY with `--dangerously-skip-permissions` plus a curated `--tools` list. The subprocess **still** displays a `"Bypass Permissions confirmation"` dialog at startup. The orchestrator's idle-watchdog auto-presses `enter`, but the prompt loops — Claude Code expects an actual selection, not a bare enter — and after a few rounds the PTY exits with code 1.

Net effect: every dispatched coding/research task fails before doing any work. From the user side, the agent says "I'll research X" then nothing happens; eventually the coordinator surfaces:

```
[SwarmCoordinator] Idle watchdog: "<task>-1" — PTY session no longer exists, marking as stopped
[SwarmCoordinator] checkAllTasksComplete: sessions are terminal but acceptance failed — thread task-<id> | failed goals: <goal>=failed
```

## Reproduction

1. Web chat or Telegram → ask Chen to research anything that triggers the orchestrator dispatch path:
   *"Search for B2B logistics companies in California with 50–500 employees that haven't adopted AI yet."*
2. Watch logs:
   ```
   [PTYService/Worker] Spawning session { type: 'claude', name: 'coding-... ' }
   [PTYService/Worker] Starting PTY session { command: 'claude', args: '--dangerously-skip-permissions --tools Read,Grep,…' }
   [PTYService/Worker] PTY session started { pid: ... }
   [PTYService/Worker] Sent input to session { input: '# Workspace\n…' }
   [PTYService/Worker] Sent special key { key: 'enter' }
   [PTYService/Worker] Blocking prompt requires user intervention {
     promptType: 'permission',
     prompt: 'Bypass Permissions confirmation'
   }
   [PTYService/Worker] Sent special key { key: 'enter' }    ← repeats 2-3×
   [PTYService/Worker] PTY session exited { exitCode: 1 }
   ```
3. Coordinator marks task failed; user sees no work done.

## Root cause

`--dangerously-skip-permissions` is a Claude Code flag that **promises** to skip the per-tool permission ask, but on first invocation the CLI shows a one-time confirmation gate ("are you sure you want to bypass permissions?") that the orchestrator's automated `enter` press doesn't satisfy. The CLI is interpreting `enter` as "show me the choices again" rather than "yes, confirmed."

The orchestrator's blocking-prompt detector sees the prompt, fires `key: enter`, sees the prompt again, fires `enter` again, and gives up after the third round. Then PTY exits.

## Suggested fixes

1. **Pre-confirm the bypass** out-of-band before spawning. Run `claude config set --global dangerouslySkipPermissionsAcknowledged true` once on first orchestrator boot (or detect the missing ack and run it). Then `--dangerously-skip-permissions` won't prompt.

2. **Match the actual prompt's accept key**. `enter` may not be the correct dismiss key — most CLI confirmations want `y` + `enter` or arrow-then-enter. Audit Claude Code's actual prompt and send the right sequence.

3. **Detect this specific failure mode and surface a real error** instead of silent task-failed. Right now the user has no way to know the subprocess is stuck on a permission dialog vs actually running.

4. **Fall back to a non-prompting agent type** (codex, e.g.) when the claude path repeatedly hits this gate.

## Why this matters

The orchestrator dispatch path is the entire reason `BROWSER_ACTION`, `USE_SKILL`, and the coding-agent flow exist. With this gate blocking every spawn, users with `PARALLAX_DEFAULT_AGENT_TYPE=claude` get **zero** completed tasks — the system looks broken on every "do X for me" request.

Combined with #7362 (capability denial), users are double-blocked: even after the agent agrees to dispatch, the dispatch fails.

## Reproduction

## Root cause

The current handler shape:

```ts
bot.on("message", async (ctx) => {
  // ... build system + history string ...
  const response = await modelRuntime.useModel(ModelType.TEXT_LARGE, {
    prompt: `${systemPrompt}\n\nConversation:\n${conv}\n\n${char.name}:`,
  });

});
```

Direct `useModel` skips:
- `runtime.composeState()` — no providers contribute context
- Action selection — no tool-use turns
- `runtime.processActions()` — no dispatch
- Memory write — `createMemory()` is never called for inbound or outbound
- Event emission — `EventType.MESSAGE_RECEIVED` and `MESSAGE_SENT` never fire, so any subscriber (analytics, training trajectories, escalation routing) is blind to Telegram traffic

## Why the wrapper exists

A comment at `packages/app-core/src/runtime/eliza.ts:531-533` explains:
> *"Ensure Telegram bot is polling. The upstream plugin's `bot.launch()` is not awaited and silently fails on bun/Windows. We create a standalone Telegraf instance with proper lifecycle management."*

So the wrapper was added to work around #7241 (Telegraf launch under Bun) and #7240 (token bridge). But the implementation went further than necessary — instead of just owning the Telegraf instance and forwarding inbound messages into the runtime, it implemented its own simplified "ask LLM, reply text" loop.

## Fix

Refactor the wrapper's message handler to forward inbound messages through the agent runtime, mirroring what `@elizaos/plugin-telegram/src/messageManager.ts` does:

1. Build a proper `Memory` object (entityId, roomId, worldId, agentId, content.text, source: "telegram", channelType, createdAt).
2. `await runtime.ensureConnection({ entityId, roomId, source: "telegram", ... })` so room/world state exists.
3. `await runtime.createMemory(memory, "messages")` so it lands in the inbound stream.
4. `runtime.emitEvent(EventType.MESSAGE_RECEIVED, { runtime, message: memory, callback })` where callback dispatches `ctx.reply()` for each response chunk.

Estimated ~200 lines of plumbing — most of it boilerplate Memory/room construction that can be lifted from the upstream `messageManager.ts` directly.

## Why this matters

Users assume their Telegram bot is the same agent as the web chat. With the current wrapper, Telegram is essentially a watered-down chatbot that can't do work. Anything the user asks Chen to *do* via Telegram will silently fail or just be described as text without execution.

Combined with #7240, #7241, #7245, the Telegram path has been on a long tail of regressions; this is the architectural one that gates feature parity.

## Environment

- bun 1.3.13
- milady on `alice` post-PR-105
- Discovered when user asked "i need my telegram bot to be able to do all of these too" (browser actions, tasks, memory) and confirmed via log inspection that the wrapper never invokes `processActions`.1e:Tc6c,## Summary

`packages/app-core/src/hooks/useActivityEvents.ts` subscribes to three WebSocket event streams (`pty-session-event`, `proactive-message`, `agent_event`) and calls `setEvents([...bufferRef.current])` on **every** event. When multiple events arrive in the same tick — common during code-task spawns, multi-step actions, or chatty proactive flows — React fires N re-renders, which the user sees as the Activity panel flickering.

## Reproduction

1. Open the dashboard, watch the right-side Activity panel.
2. Trigger any flow that emits multiple `agent_event`s rapidly (start a code task with sub-steps, or run anything that emits proactive nudges in quick succession).
3. Activity panel visibly flickers / re-renders rapidly.

Frequency scales with WS event volume — light usage might never trigger it; heavy use makes it constant.

## Root cause

```ts
const pushEvent = useCallback((entry) => {
  const event = { ...entry, id: makeEventId() };
  const buf = bufferRef.current;
  buf.unshift(event);
  if (buf.length > RING_BUFFER_CAP) buf.length = RING_BUFFER_CAP;
  setEvents([...buf]);  // ← new array reference every event
}, []);
```

Each `setEvents([...buf])` allocates a new top-level array reference, so React's bailout doesn't kick in. With 3 active WS subscriptions firing in bursts, you get unboundedly many renders per second. No batching, no rAF coalescing, no debounce.

## Fix (verified locally)

Coalesce bursts into one render via `requestAnimationFrame`:

```ts
const flushHandleRef = useRef<number | null>(null);

const pushEvent = useCallback((entry) => {
  const event = { ...entry, id: makeEventId() };
  const buf = bufferRef.current;
  buf.unshift(event);
  if (buf.length > RING_BUFFER_CAP) buf.length = RING_BUFFER_CAP;
  if (flushHandleRef.current !== null) return;       // already scheduled
  flushHandleRef.current = requestAnimationFrame(() => {
    flushHandleRef.current = null;
    setEvents([...bufferRef.current]);
  });
}, []);

// cancel pending flush on unmount
useEffect(() => () => {
  if (flushHandleRef.current !== null) {
    cancelAnimationFrame(flushHandleRef.current);
  }
}, []);

// clearEvents also cancels pending flush
const clearEvents = useCallback(() => {
  bufferRef.current = [];
  if (flushHandleRef.current !== null) {
    cancelAnimationFrame(flushHandleRef.current);
    flushHandleRef.current = null;
  }
  setEvents([]);
}, []);
```

After patch: at most one render per animation frame regardless of how many events fire. Visible flicker eliminated. Tested locally during a multi-step agent run.

## Why rAF and not debounce

- `requestAnimationFrame` is the right cadence for visible UI updates — anything finer is wasted work, anything coarser feels laggy.
- Survives backgrounded tabs (rAF pauses them, which is the correct behavior).
- No timeout magic numbers to tune.

## Why this matters

Subtle but persistent flicker is a "the app feels broken" UX signal even when functionally everything works. With the upcoming hyperscape / agent-orchestrator flows producing more event volume, this gets worse, not better.

### Bug A: Agent denies having tools it actually has

A user asks Chen via Telegram (or web chat) to add a task to her task manager. Chen replies:

> *"just to be clear — i don't have a task manager or memory between sessions, so i can't save it on my end. but you can keep this as your task… copy that somewhere you'll actually see it."*

This is **wrong**:

- `eliza/packages/typescript/src/features/advanced-capabilities/actions/createTask.ts:103` defines a `CREATE_TASK` action: *"Create an autonomous trigger task (interval, once, or cron)"*.
- `eliza/plugins/plugin-cron/typescript/src/actions/` has full `create-cron`, `list-crons`, `delete-cron`, `update-cron`, `run-cron` implementations.
- `plugin-sql` has a real `tasks` table (we see queries against it on every boot — the `__db_ready_probe__` line in #7222 hits it).
- Long-term memory is a real capability — `entity_identities`, `fact_candidates`, the trajectories table, `longTermMemoryProvider`. Per CLAUDE.md: *"Trajectory persistence is on by default. Every turn lands in the `trajectories` table."*

The agent has all of this and still tells the user "I don't have it." That's a worst-case UX failure: capable system, agent unaware of its capabilities, polite-sounding lie surfaced to the user. The user has no way to know the system can actually do the thing.

#### Likely root cause

The system prompt and `actions` provider don't list these capabilities to the model. The agent picks up `CREATE_TASK` only if (a) the action's plugin is in the auto-enable map, (b) the action gets surfaced in the prompt's `Available actions` block, (c) the character's `system` doesn't actively suppress it. On a default install at least one of those gates is failing.

#### Suggested fix

1. **Auto-enable** the cron / task-creation plugin by default (or include `CREATE_TASK` in the always-on action set).
2. **Inject capability hints into the system prompt** — something like *"You have a persistent task manager (CREATE_TASK), long-term memory (trajectories + entity_identities), and can schedule work. Don't claim otherwise."*
3. **Add a fallback**: when the agent emits a refusal that mentions "no memory" / "no task manager" / "no persistence" and the runtime has the corresponding capability, log it (so devs notice) and ideally re-prompt with the capability list.

### Bug B: Hyperscape app overwrites `agents.list` on install

When the Hyperscape app/plugin is installed (`@hyperscape/plugin-hyperscape` + `@elizaos/app-hyperscape`), its bootstrap step **replaces** `agents.list` in `~/.milady/milady.json` with a single `"Hyperscape Explorer"` entry — wiping out the user's existing character (Chen, in our case). After install, the user opens the chat and the default agent is no longer who they onboarded with.

Reproduction:

1. Onboard fresh, pick Chen.
2. `cat ~/.milady/milady.json` — `agents.list` either absent (preset rebuilds Chen) or contains a Chen entry. `ui.presetId === "chen"`.
3. Install Hyperscape (env vars `HYPERSCAPE_SERVER_URL`, `HYPERSCAPE_API_URL`, `HYPERSCAPE_CLIENT_URL` written; plugins enabled).
4. `cat ~/.milady/milady.json` — `agents.list` is now `[{ name: "Hyperscape Explorer", bio: [...], topics: ["hyperscape","osrs",...], ... }]`. **Chen is gone.** `ui.presetId` still says `"chen"` but it's ignored when `agents.list` is populated.
5. Restart milady. Default chat agent is "Hyperscape Explorer" — an OSRS adventurer the user never asked for.

Workaround: delete `agents.list` from `~/.milady/milady.json`, restart. The runtime rebuilds from `presetId` and Chen comes back.

#### Suggested fix

App / plugin install paths must **not** silently mutate `agents.list`. Two acceptable behaviors:

1. **Append** a new agent entry rather than replace.
2. **Provide a sample/demo character separately** (e.g., a "Hyperscape Demo" preset the user can pick from a gallery) instead of writing it into the live agent list.

Either way, an install step should never destroy user character config without consent.

### Why I bundled them

These hit the user in the same flow: they install Hyperscape (or another app that does this), their agent silently changes, the new agent doesn't know what it can or can't do, and on the very next user message the agent confidently denies having a task manager. Both bugs stem from the same general pattern — system writes config the user doesn't see, agent doesn't introspect its own runtime state.

## API drift fixes (alpha.3 → alpha.537)

The standalone \`peerDependencies\` pinned \`@elizaos/core: 2.0.0-alpha.3\`. The monorepo is at alpha.537, and the core API has moved in two specific ways the slack plugin needed updates for:

- **\`State.recentMessagesData\` typing.** Providers in \`channelState.ts\`, \`memberList.ts\`, \`workspaceInfo.ts\` read \`state?.recentMessagesData\`, which is now typed as the broader \`StateValue\` union (\`string | number | bigint | true | object\`) rather than \`Memory[]\` directly. Cast the field to \`Memory[] | undefined\` at the read site so \`validateActionKeywords\` / \`validateActionRegex\` get the expected shape. Behavior unchanged.
- **\`MentionContext\` shape.** \`service.ts\` was constructing \`{ isMention: true }\`; the type now requires \`isReply\` and \`isThread\` too. Filled with \`false\` for the mention-only path. Behavior unchanged for the existing mention handling.

## Context

Fixes the root cause behind the May 2 `CACHE_ENABLED=false` hotfix:
`CacheClient` was a module-level singleton whose lazy-opened Redis socket
got bound to the first request's I/O context on Cloudflare Workers,
killing the worker on subsequent requests with `Cannot perform I/O on
behalf of a different request`.

Rather than just fix the cache singleton (étape 2 plan, ALS facade with
documented dette), the user chose **Clean Architecture** (étape 3) — no
intermediate dette, layered domain/application/infrastructure, repository
pattern, cache as decorator. See ADR:
[docs/architecture/clean-architecture-migration.md](cloud/docs/architecture/clean-architecture-migration.md).

3. **`/types/nodes.json` multi-entry merge** — Gmail/Discord listed once per versioned-node class; Set-accumulate across same-name entries (fixes a `flatMap` bug that picked the first entry's versions only).
4. **Missing `parameters.authentication`** when credentials attached — back-fill from `displayOptions.show.authentication`.
5. **Output-field references with case mismatches** — deterministic case-fix against the upstream node's actual output schema.
6. **Bracket-notation expressions `\$json[\"X\"]`** — regex extended to catch the bracket form, not just dot-notation.
7. **Aggregation-source-field hallucinations** — Summarize node's `field` parameter validated against the upstream source node's output schema.
8. **Static-schema vs runtime-shape mismatch** — Gmail simple-mode override beats static schema (node returns flat fields when `format: simple`, deeply-nested when `format: full`).
9. **Node-name collisions** — auto-rename with `(N)` suffix.
10. **Connection edges to non-existent nodes** — drop + log.

### What's new

- **`src/utils/validateAndRepair.ts`** (561 lines) — the orchestrator. Walks every node, runs each validator, applies repairs in-place. Returns `{ workflow, repairs: [], errors: [] }`. Pure function — no n8n calls.

- **`src/utils/inferSyntheticOutputSchema.ts`** (144 lines) — when an upstream node has no static output schema, infer one from its `parameters.fieldsToOutput` or similar. Used by the case-fix and aggregation-source validators.

- **`src/utils/api.ts`** (48 lines added) — `/types/nodes.json` parsing fix: aggregate `typeVersion` arrays across all entries with the same `name`, instead of taking the first entry's.

- **`src/utils/catalog.ts`** (47 lines added) — `clampTypeVersion(node, runtimeVersions)` helper.

- **`src/utils/outputSchema.ts`** (16 lines added) — exported helper for case-folded field lookup, used by the validator.

- **`src/utils/generation.ts`** (77 lines added) — \"catalog facts\" block injected into the prompt: per-node-type, lists allowed `typeVersion`s and required parameters. Helps the model produce correct workflows on first generation, reducing repair work.

- **`src/services/n8n-workflow-service.ts`** (92 lines added) — wiring: call `validateAndRepair` after generation, inject repair feedback into a retry prompt if errors remain, retry up to N times. Backs off cleanly if all retries still have errors and surfaces the residual error list to the host.

- **`src/prompts/workflowGeneration.ts`** (45 lines added) — instructional rules added to the prompt explaining each anti-hallucination invariant in plain English (model accuracy improves measurably when the rule is also stated in the prompt, not just enforced post-hoc).

- **`__tests__/unit/validateAndRepair.test.ts`** (503 lines, all new) — covers each of the 10 hallucination classes plus the retry loop wiring. Pure unit tests — no live n8n required.

### Why a deterministic pass

The repair-via-LLM-retry path alone has three failure modes:
- It's slow (extra round-trips, often two or three).
- The model sometimes \"fixes\" the wrong thing (changes a node type when the issue was just a typeVersion).
- It can introduce new hallucinations while fixing the old ones (cycle).

A deterministic pass with the catalog + runtime as ground truth is faster, cheaper, and has a bounded blast radius. Repair-via-LLM still runs **after** the deterministic pass for residual errors the deterministic pass can't fix on its own.

Adds an optional `preferredProviders` array to the `keywordExtraction` request, biasing the model toward provider-specific keywords when the host knows which integrations are actually available.

### Why

Today the keyword-extraction LLM call sees the user's prompt with no awareness of which providers are connected. So when a user asks for *"send a daily email summary"*, the extracted keywords might include generic terms like `email`, `send`, `daily` — but if the host has Gmail connected and the model didn't bias toward that, the downstream node-search step misses the Gmail-specific candidates.

With `preferredProviders: ["Gmail", "Discord"]`, the prompt now hints "the user has Gmail and Discord connected — prefer keywords specific to those when ambiguous." Empirically this raises the rate of Gmail-specific node hits (`gmailTrigger`, `gmail.send`) on prompts that don't explicitly say "Gmail."

### What's new

- **`KeywordExtractionRequest.preferredProviders?: string[]`** type field (`src/types/index.ts`).
- **Service-side wiring** (`src/services/n8n-workflow-service.ts`) — accepts the array via existing service-call options, forwards it into the prompt assembler.
- **Prompt assembly update** (`src/utils/generation.ts`) — appends a `Preferred providers: <list>` line to the keyword-extraction system prompt when the array is non-empty.
- **Unit test** (`__tests__/unit/generation.test.ts`) — covers the new prompt-text branch.

Optional + backwards-compatible: callers that don't pass it get today's behavior unchanged.

<!-- /greptile_comment -->2a:T88f,## Summary

Adds `injectMissingCredentialBlocks` — a deterministic post-generation pass that walks every node in the generated workflow, checks whether it requires credentials, and injects the correct credential block from the host's resolved credential map.

This catches the common LLM failure where the model omits the `credentials` block on a node entirely (often because the prompt instructs it to leave credentials empty for the host to inject — see #20 — and the model then forgets that the host *will* inject them and produces a workflow that's structurally credential-less).

### What's new

- **`injectMissingCredentialBlocks(workflow, resolvedCredentials)`** in `src/utils/workflow.ts` — pure function. For each node, looks at its `type` + `typeVersion`, consults the credential resolver's output to find the credentialId, and writes a `credentials: { <credentialType>: { id, name } }` block if one is missing.

- **Service-side wiring** in `src/services/n8n-workflow-service.ts` — calls the new helper after generation and before deployment. No-op if all nodes already have credential blocks (which is the happy-path case).

### Why deterministic

The repair path could ask the LLM to add credentials, but:
- It's slow (extra round-trip).
- The model frequently picks the wrong credential type or hallucinates IDs.
- The host already knows the right answer (it's the same credential the user picked when configuring the connector).

A deterministic pass with the host's credential map as ground truth is faster, cheaper, and more correct.

## Stacking

**Depends on #20** (RuntimeContextProvider + prompt hardening). The credential-rule prompt change in PR #20 is what creates the failure mode this PR catches; they should land together.

This branch was cherry-picked on top of #20's branch, so until #20 merges this PR's diff includes #20's commit. When #20 merges, this PR auto-rebases and shows only its own diff.

## Test plan

- [x] Verified live in Milady against `n8n@1.119+` — workflows that previously deployed credential-less now deploy with the right credential blocks attached.
- [ ] Reviewer: existing tests should remain green; this is purely additive.2b:T182e,## Summary

Renders the `needs_clarification` response from `POST /api/n8n/workflows/generate` (added in #7316) as an inline panel in `AutomationsView`, just below the missing-credentials banner. The user picks from a row of buttons drawn from the `connector-target-catalog` snapshot (#7315), the host calls `POST /api/n8n/workflows/resolve-clarification` with `{paramPath, value}`, and either deploys (clearing the panel and refreshing the workflow list) or chains a follow-up picker (server then channel) by surfacing the next pending clarification.

This was the planned slice-2 P5 UI surface that #7316 / #7317 made the backend for. Shipping it now closes the loop: the route + UX restoration are already on develop, but the user-facing clarification picker was missing.

## Implementation

`ClarificationPanel` renders `ChoiceWidget` directly. `ChoiceWidget`'s existing `onChoose` callback contract was already a clean direct callback — the chat round-trip via `sendActionMessage` is layered on in `MessageContent.tsx`, not in the widget itself, so the widget did not need an `onChooseDirect` prop. The clarification flow simply instantiates `ChoiceWidget` with its own callback.

`optionsForClarification` narrows the catalog snapshot per clarification kind:
- `target_server` lists one button per group.
- `target_channel` narrows to `scope.guildId` when set, then lists each text channel; if no scope is set and multiple guilds returned, the label is prefixed with the guild name to disambiguate same-named channels.
- `recipient` lists each recipient target.
- `value` / `free_text` / unmatched-platform fall through to a free-text `Input` bubble (`ClarificationFreeTextInput`) so the user can still answer when no catalog backs the question.

Cancel dismisses the panel locally without touching the server. A busy spinner suppresses re-clicks while resolve is in flight; an error string surfaces failed resolves (bad paramPath, validation rejection) without dropping the panel.

`client-n8n.ts` gains `resolveN8nClarification(request)` calling `POST /api/n8n/workflows/resolve-clarification` with the same 120s timeout as `generateN8nWorkflow` (validateAndRepair + deploy can be slow).

<!-- /greptile_comment -->2e:T1b6c,## Summary

Follow-up to #7367. That PR fixed the `useEffect` cleanup deadlock by adding the `if (!completionFiredRef.current) abort.abort()` guard, but the `active` flag race was left in place.

If `authenticated` or `ready` toggles in `useSessionAuth` while `POST /api/auth/cli-session/:id/complete` is in flight (steward token refresh, provider re-bootstrap, storage event, etc.), the cleanup runs:

- `active = false` ← still flipped unconditionally
- `abort.abort()` ← correctly skipped since #7367

The fetch eventually resolves with 200 OK and the API key is created server-side, but the success branch is gated by `if (active)` and never runs. The UI stays stuck on "Generating API Key..." indefinitely. From the user's perspective: their CLI session never completes even though the key exists in the DB.

This was flagged as a P1 by Greptile during the review of #7367 ([comment](https://github.com/elizaOS/eliza/blob/f492088f629bc43fc1b236b13066f73ee2fe67c2/cloud/apps/frontend/src/pages/auth/cli-login/page.tsx#L203-L207)) — Greptile's suggested fix addressed the abort but not the `active` flag.

## Change

Drop the `active` flag entirely:
- Remove `let active = true;`
- Remove `if (active) { ... }` wrapper around the success `setCompletion`
- Remove `if (!active) return;` from the catch
- Remove `active = false;` from the cleanup
- Keep the `if (!completionFiredRef.current) abort.abort()` guard from #7367

`completionFiredRef` already enforces a single POST per session lifecycle, so unconditional `setCompletion` is safe in both success and catch paths. The `apiFetch` `signal` still fires when the legitimate timeout (`COMPLETE_TIMEOUT_MS = 30_000`) trips, which is the only case the cleanup needs to abort.

## Testing

Wired up vitest in `cloud/apps/frontend` (no test infra existed). Added `cloud/apps/frontend/src/pages/auth/cli-login/page.test.tsx` that:

1. Mounts `<CliLoginContent />` with `useSessionAuth` returning `{ ready: true, authenticated: true }`.
2. Asserts the POST is in flight ("Generating API Key" visible).
3. Flickers `authenticated` to `false` then back to `true` (re-renders) while the POST is held by a Deferred — this is exactly the auth-state toggle that triggers the bug.
4. Resolves the POST with 200 + `{ keyPrefix }`.
5. Asserts the UI advances to the "Authentication Complete!" success state with the key prefix visible.

- On `origin/develop`: test FAILS — \`expected null not to be null\` on the success-state lookup. UI stuck on "Generating API Key".
- With this fix: test PASSES.

<!-- /greptile_comment -->2f:Tce9,## Summary

Lets the host pass an opaque routing block (Discord channelId/guildId, Telegram chatId, Slack channelId/teamId, etc.) to the runtime context provider, so the LLM can target "this channel" / "back to me" without the user having to name an ID.

## Why

When a workflow is generated from inside a Discord DM ("every weekday 9am post the day's calendar agenda back to this channel"), the model has no way to know which Discord channel the user means. Today the generated `Discord Send` node ends up with a blank `channelId` or a placeholder. With `triggerContext` in the provider input, the host can derive the routing block from the inbound message's `MessageMetadata` and emit a fact line like:

> This workflow was prompted from Discord channel #foo (id 9876543210) in "Cozy Devs" (id 1234567890). When the user references "this channel" or "back to here", target that channel ID.

…which the LLM picks up as a `## Runtime Facts` line. The plugin itself stays prompt-agnostic — it just plumbs the field through.

## Changes

- **New `TriggerContext` interface** (`src/types/index.ts`):
  ```ts
  export interface TriggerContext {
    source?: string;
    discord?: { channelId?: string; guildId?: string; threadId?: string };
    telegram?: { chatId?: string | number; threadId?: string | number };
    slack?: { channelId?: string; teamId?: string };
    resolvedNames?: { channel?: string; server?: string };
  }
  ```
- `RuntimeContextProviderInput.triggerContext?: TriggerContext` — additive, forward-compatible. Hosts that don't know about it just omit the field.
- `N8nWorkflowService.generateWorkflowDraft(prompt, opts?)` and `modifyWorkflowDraft(existing, request, opts?)` accept `{ triggerContext?: TriggerContext }`. Threaded into both `fetchRuntimeContext` calls (generate + modify paths).

## Backward compatibility

100% additive. Existing callers pass nothing, behavior unchanged. The host emits the trigger fact line into the existing `facts[]` array — the plugin's prompt-builder doesn't need to know about the wording.

## Depends on

**Stacked on #20** (RuntimeContextProvider extension point). Until that merges, this PR's diff includes the dependency. Once #20 merges, GitHub auto-rebases and the diff collapses to just the additive `TriggerContext` + opt argument.

## Test plan

- [ ] Calling `generateWorkflowDraft(prompt)` (no opts) produces the same workflow as today.
- [ ] Calling `generateWorkflowDraft(prompt, { triggerContext: { source: "discord", discord: { channelId, guildId } } })` threads the trigger context to the registered runtime context provider's `getRuntimeContext` input.
- [ ] Same for `modifyWorkflowDraft(workflow, request, { triggerContext })`.

<!-- /greptile_comment -->33:Td77,## Summary

Adds a `RuntimeContextProvider` extension point so embedding apps can inject runtime facts (current time, agent identity, available channels, user prefs, etc.) into the workflow-generation prompt, plus three correctness fixes in the prompt itself that consistently bit us in production.

### What's new

1. **`RuntimeContextProvider` interface** (`src/types/index.ts`) — pluggable provider that the host app registers on the service. Returns a string of context that's appended to the system prompt before generation. Lets downstream apps surface things the plugin can't know on its own (e.g. "the current Discord channel is #general", "today is Sunday").

2. **Service wiring** (`src/services/n8n-workflow-service.ts`) — accepts the provider via constructor option, calls it during prompt assembly, and falls back to no-op if the host doesn't provide one. Backwards-compatible with all existing callers.

3. **Prompt hardening** (`src/prompts/workflowGeneration.ts`) — three correctness rules added:
   - **Credentials rule:** explicit instruction to leave `credentials` empty in node JSON; the host injects them post-generation.
   - **Runtime facts rule:** instruction to use the `RuntimeContextProvider` output as ground truth for time/identity/channel/etc., rather than guessing.
   - **Output-field rule:** instruction to reference output fields with exact case as they appear in the schema (e.g. `subject`, not `Subject`).

4. **Generation glue** (`src/utils/generation.ts`) — passes the runtime-context string into the prompt assembler.

### Why these changes

The prompt today produces correct workflows for simple cases but the model regularly hallucinates:
- credentials inside node JSON (causing duplicate-credential errors after host injection),
- runtime facts (the model assumes "now" is its training cutoff and writes stale cron expressions),
- output field names with wrong casing (which then fail when downstream nodes reference them).

The provider extension also unblocks downstream apps that have richer runtime state than the plugin itself can know.

## Test plan

## What changes

- **`extractFirstBalancedJsonValue`** (new helper, exported for unit-testability) walks every `{`/`[` opener in the response text, walks each candidate to its matching close bracket (respecting JSON string escapes), and returns the first slice that round-trips through `JSON.parse`. Tolerates:
  - prose-prefix (`Here's the JSON: {…}`)
  - bracketed-prefix (`[note] {…}` — markdown checkboxes, citations)
  - concatenated/duplicated payloads
- **Code-fence stripping** now accepts 1+ backticks with an optional `json` label instead of requiring strict triple backticks. Models occasionally emit single-backtick fences when they hit a token budget mid-fence.
- **`extractResponsesOutputText`** returns the first non-empty source (`output_text` → `output[]` → `choices[]`) instead of concatenating all three, which produced doubled bodies (`{...}\n\`\`\`\n\`\`\`json\n{...}`) that choked `JSON.parse` after fence-strip.
- **Tests:** 5 new cases in `text-object-models.real.test.ts` covering single-backtick fence, doubled-glue, prose prefix, bracketed-prose prefix, and structured-message recovery.

## Why mirror

The standalone PR (#18 on elizaos-plugins/plugin-elizacloud) was opened before the plugin migration into the monorepo. The fix is needed in this tree to actually ship to users. Closing the standalone PR once this merges.

<!-- /greptile_comment -->36:T834,## Summary

`runtime.getSetting('SOME_KEY')` is the documented way for plugins to read agent-scoped configuration (see plugin-discord, plugin-twitter, etc.). Currently the only delivery channel for those values is `process.env` behind the hard-coded `GETSETTING_ENV_ALLOWLIST` in `packages/agent/src/runtime/eliza.ts`.

This adds a typed `settings?: Record<string, string|number|boolean|null>` field to `AgentConfig` (in `packages/shared/src/config/types.agents.ts`) and merges it into the derived base settings inside `buildCharacterFromConfig()`. Per-agent values win over derived defaults so operators can override capability-derived settings from config when needed.

## Motivation

Field evidence: a self-hosted milady-cloud agent (`nyx`) was unable to deliver `DISCORD_AUTO_REPLY` through agent config and had to monkey-patch the runtime allowlist. With this change, the workaround is unnecessary, and other plugin authors get a clean per-agent config surface without having to lobby for new keys to be added to a hardcoded allowlist.

## Implementation

1. Add typed `settings` field to `AgentConfig` in `packages/shared/src/config/types.agents.ts`.
2. In `buildCharacterFromConfig()`, merge `agentEntry.settings` on top of derived `baseSettings` so per-agent overrides win over capability defaults.
3. Skip silently if `agentEntry.settings` is missing or non-object. Filter undefined values (treat as opt-out).

## Tests

`packages/agent/src/runtime/build-character-from-config.test.ts`:

- ✅ preserves agent entry settings on character.settings
- ✅ does not clobber derived base settings when agent entry has none
- ✅ per-agent overrides win over derived defaults
- ✅ undefined-valued keys are opt-outs
- ✅ non-object settings do not throw
- ✅ accepts numeric and boolean values

## Risk / Scope

- Low. Pure addition. No existing tests changed. Existing behavior for configs without `settings` field is byte-identical.
- Secret-handling unaffected (still goes through the existing `secrets` channel and env filter).

<summary>Changelog</summary>
<p><em>Sourced from <a href="https://github.com/axios/axios/blob/v1.x/CHANGELOG.md">axios's changelog</a>.</em></p>
<blockquote>
<h2>v1.15.0 - April 7, 2026</h2>
<p>This release delivers two critical security patches targeting header injection and SSRF via proxy bypass, adds official runtime support for Deno and Bun, and includes significant CI security hardening.</p>
<h2>🔒 Security Fixes</h2>
<ul>
<li>
<p><strong>Header Injection (CRLF):</strong> Rejects any header value containing <code>\r</code> or <code>\n</code> characters to block CRLF injection chains that could be used to exfiltrate cloud metadata (IMDS). Behavior change: headers with CR/LF now throw <code>&quot;Invalid character in header content&quot;</code>. (<strong><a href="https://redirect.github.com/axios/axios/issues/10660">#10660</a></strong>)</p>
</li>
<li>
<p><strong>SSRF via <code>no_proxy</code> Bypass:</strong> Introduces a <code>shouldBypassProxy</code> helper that normalises hostnames (strips trailing dots, handles bracketed IPv6) before evaluating <code>no_proxy</code>/<code>NO_PROXY</code> rules, closing a gap that could cause loopback or internal hosts to be inadvertently proxied. (<strong><a href="https://redirect.github.com/axios/axios/issues/10661">#10661</a></strong>)</p>
</li>
</ul>
<h2>🚀 New Features</h2>
<ul>
<li><strong>Deno &amp; Bun Runtime Support:</strong> Added full smoke test suites for Deno and Bun, with CI workflows that run both runtimes before any release is cut. (<strong><a href="https://redirect.github.com/axios/axios/issues/10652">#10652</a></strong>)</li>
</ul>
<h2>🐛 Bug Fixes</h2>
<ul>
<li><strong>Node.js v22 Compatibility:</strong> Replaced deprecated <code>url.parse()</code> calls with the WHATWG <code>URL</code>/<code>URLSearchParams</code> API across examples, sandbox, and tests, eliminating <code>DEP0169</code> deprecation warnings on Node.js v22+. (<strong><a href="https://redirect.github.com/axios/axios/issues/10625">#10625</a></strong>)</li>
</ul>
<h2>🔧 Maintenance &amp; Chores</h2>
<ul>
<li>
<p><strong>CI Security Hardening:</strong> Added <a href="https://github.com/zizmorcore/zizmor">zizmor</a> GitHub Actions security scanner; switched npm publish to OIDC Trusted Publishing (removing the long-lived <code>NODE_AUTH_TOKEN</code>); pinned all action references to full commit SHAs; narrowed workflow permissions to least privilege; gated the publish step behind a dedicated <code>npm-publish</code> environment; and blocked the sponsor-block workflow from running on forks. (<strong><a href="https://redirect.github.com/axios/axios/issues/10618">#10618</a></strong>, <strong><a href="https://redirect.github.com/axios/axios/issues/10619">#10619</a></strong>, <strong><a href="https://redirect.github.com/axios/axios/issues/10627">#10627</a></strong>, <strong><a href="https://redirect.github.com/axios/axios/issues/10637">#10637</a></strong>, <strong><a href="https://redirect.github.com/axios/axios/issues/10641">#10641</a></strong>, <strong><a href="https://redirect.github.com/axios/axios/issues/10666">#10666</a></strong>)</p>
</li>
<li>
<p><strong>Docs:</strong> Clarified HTTP/2 support and the unsupported <code>httpVersion</code> option; added documentation for header case preservation; improved the <code>beforeRedirect</code> example to prevent accidental credential leakage. (<strong><a href="https://redirect.github.com/axios/axios/issues/10644">#10644</a></strong>, <strong><a href="https://redirect.github.com/axios/axios/issues/10654">#10654</a></strong>, <strong><a href="https://redirect.github.com/axios/axios/issues/10624">#10624</a></strong>)</p>
</li>
<li>
<p><strong>Dependencies:</strong> Bumped <code>picomatch</code>, <code>handlebars</code>, <code>serialize-javascript</code>, <code>vite</code> (×3), <code>denoland/setup-deno</code>, and 4 additional dev dependencies to latest versions. (<strong><a href="https://redirect.github.com/axios/axios/issues/10564">#10564</a></strong>, <strong><a href="https://redirect.github.com/axios/axios/issues/10565">#10565</a></strong>, <strong><a href="https://redirect.github.com/axios/axios/issues/10567">#10567</a></strong>, <strong><a href="https://redirect.github.com/axios/axios/issues/10568">#10568</a></strong>, <strong><a href="https://redirect.github.com/axios/axios/issues/10572">#10572</a></strong>, <strong><a href="https://redirect.github.com/axios/axios/issues/10574">#10574</a></strong>, <strong><a href="https://redirect.github.com/axios/axios/issues/10663">#10663</a></strong>, <strong><a href="https://redirect.github.com/axios/axios/issues/10664">#10664</a></strong>, <strong><a href="https://redirect.github.com/axios/axios/issues/10665">#10665</a></strong>, <strong><a href="https://redirect.github.com/axios/axios/issues/10669">#10669</a></strong>, <strong><a href="https://redirect.github.com/axios/axios/issues/10670">#10670</a></strong>)</p>

<h2>6.0.171</h2>
<h3>Patch Changes</h3>
<ul>
<li>
<p>48f842a: fix(ai): enforce <code>callOptionsSchema</code> at runtime in <code>ToolLoopAgent</code></p>
<p><code>ToolLoopAgentSettings.callOptionsSchema</code> was declared and documented as a runtime schema for <code>options</code>, but <code>tool-loop-agent.ts</code> never invoked it. Any invariant a developer encoded in the schema was silently bypassed at runtime, and unchecked <code>options</code> flowed straight into <code>prepareCall</code> and any <code>instructions</code> template that interpolated them.</p>
<p><code>ToolLoopAgent.prepareCall</code> now validates caller-supplied <code>options</code> against <code>callOptionsSchema</code> (when set) via <code>safeValidateTypes</code>, throwing <code>InvalidArgumentError</code> on failure before forwarding to <code>prepareCall</code> / <code>generateText</code> / <code>streamText</code>.</p>
</li>
<li>
<p>a727da4: chore: ensure consistent import handling and avoid import duplicates or cycles</p>
</li>
<li>
<p>5fee301: fix(mcp): prevent prototype pollution by using secureJsonParse</p>
</li>
<li>
<p>Updated dependencies [a727da4]</p>
<ul>
<li><code>@​ai-sdk/provider-utils</code><a href="https://github.com/4"><code>@​4</code></a>.0.25</li>
<li><code>@​ai-sdk/provider</code><a href="https://github.com/3"><code>@​3</code></a>.0.10</li>
<li><code>@​ai-sdk/gateway</code><a href="https://github.com/3"><code>@​3</code></a>.0.106</li>
</ul>
</li>
</ul>

<blockquote>
<h2><a href="https://github.com/uuidjs/uuid/compare/v13.0.0...v14.0.0">14.0.0</a> (2026-04-19)</h2>
<h3>Security</h3>
<ul>
<li>Fixes <a href="https://github.com/uuidjs/uuid/security/advisories/GHSA-w5hq-g745-h8pq">GHSA-w5hq-g745-h8pq</a>: <code>v3()</code>, <code>v5()</code>, and <code>v6()</code> did not validate that writes would remain within the bounds of a caller-supplied buffer, allowing out-of-bounds writes when an invalid <code>offset</code> was provided. A <code>RangeError</code> is now thrown if <code>offset &lt; 0</code> or <code>offset + 16 &gt; buf.length</code>.</li>
</ul>
<h3>⚠ BREAKING CHANGES</h3>
<ul>
<li><code>crypto</code> is now expected to be globally defined (requires node@20+) (<a href="https://redirect.github.com/uuidjs/uuid/issues/935">#935</a>)</li>
<li>drop node@18 support (<a href="https://redirect.github.com/uuidjs/uuid/issues/934">#934</a>)</li>
<li>upgrade minimum supported TypeScript version to 5.4.3, in keeping with the project's policy of supporting TypeScript versions released within the last two years</li>
</ul>

<h2><a href="https://github.com/uuidjs/uuid/compare/v13.0.0...v14.0.0">14.0.0</a> (2026-04-19)</h2>
<h3>Security</h3>
<ul>
<li>Fixes <a href="https://github.com/uuidjs/uuid/security/advisories/GHSA-w5hq-g745-h8pq">GHSA-w5hq-g745-h8pq</a>: <code>v3()</code>, <code>v5()</code>, and <code>v6()</code> did not validate that writes would remain within the bounds of a caller-supplied buffer, allowing out-of-bounds writes when an invalid <code>offset</code> was provided. A <code>RangeError</code> is now thrown if <code>offset &lt; 0</code> or <code>offset + 16 &gt; buf.length</code>.</li>
</ul>
<h3>⚠ BREAKING CHANGES</h3>
<ul>
<li><code>crypto</code> is now expected to be globally defined (requires node@20+) (<a href="https://redirect.github.com/uuidjs/uuid/issues/935">#935</a>)</li>
<li>drop node@18 support (<a href="https://redirect.github.com/uuidjs/uuid/issues/934">#934</a>)</li>
<li>upgrade minimum supported TypeScript version to 5.4.3, in keeping with the project's policy of supporting TypeScript versions released within the last two years</li>
</ul>

<h3>Greptile Summary</h3>

Dependabot batch update across 8 directories covering 17 packages, including security patches for `axios` (SSRF, header injection), `handlebars`, `postcss`, and `path-to-regexp`, alongside several major-version bumps that carry breaking changes.

- **`ai` v4 → v6** (`plugin-ollama`): Two major versions skipped while `@ai-sdk/ui-utils` stays at `^1.2.8` (a v4-era package), creating a peer-dependency mismatch that is likely to cause type errors or runtime failures.
- **`uuid` v9/v11 → v14** (three plugins): `uuid@14` requires Node ≥ 20 and is ESM-only; consuming code running on Node 18 or using `require('uuid')` will break.
- **`vite` v5 → v8** (`plugin-action-bench` frontend): Vite 8 defaults to the Rolldown bundler and has breaking config changes that may silently break the frontend build.

<h3>Confidence Score: 3/5</h3>

Not safe to merge as-is — three major-version bumps carry breaking changes that need validation before landing on develop.

Multiple P1 findings: the ai v4→v6 jump with a mismatched @ai-sdk/ui-utils, uuid v14 dropping Node 18 and CJS, and vite v5→v8 changing the default bundler. The security patches in the same PR are beneficial, but the breaking major bumps prevent a confident merge without additional compatibility testing.

<h3>Greptile Summary</h3>

This PR fixes the CLI login deadlock on elizacloud.ai by making two coordinated changes: (1) flipping `workers-hono-auth` to prefer `STEWARD_JWT_SECRET` over the legacy `STEWARD_SESSION_SECRET` so the Worker's JWT verifier matches the Steward server, and (2) routing all browser session-cookie calls through the same-origin Cloudflare Pages proxy instead of directly to `api.elizacloud.ai` so the resulting cookie stays visible to all subsequent API calls.

- **P1 — stale cookie cleanup gap**: `ELIZA_CLOUD_COOKIE_HOSTS` omits `dev.elizacloud.ai`, which was covered by the old `ELIZA_CLOUD_PROXIED_HOSTS` set. Users on that host who have existing direct-API cookies will not have them cleared on logout because `clearServerStewardSessionCookies()` never fires the DELETE against `api.elizacloud.ai` for that origin.

<h3>Confidence Score: 3/5</h3>

Safe to merge for production elizacloud.ai, but dev.elizacloud.ai users cannot fully clear stale direct-API cookies on logout until the cleanup set is corrected.

The core fixes (secret priority swap, same-origin routing) are correct and well-tested. A P1 regression exists in the logout path for dev.elizacloud.ai: the stale-cookie cleanup set omits that host despite it being covered by the old flow, meaning HttpOnly cookies on api.elizacloud.ai will persist after logout for users on dev.elizacloud.ai. This pulls the score below the P1 ceiling of 4.

cloud/packages/lib/providers/StewardProvider.tsx — ELIZA_CLOUD_COOKIE_HOSTS needs dev.elizacloud.ai added to match the coverage of the removed ELIZA_CLOUD_PROXIED_HOSTS.

<!-- /greptile_comment -->39:T1622,## Summary
- The SIWE endpoints `/api/auth/siwe/{nonce,verify}` 503 in prod because `CACHE_ENABLED="false"` is set as a hotfix (commit 3c00f8e62a) and both routes gate on `cache.isAvailable()`.
- The hotfix exists because `CacheClient` is a module-level singleton whose lazy-opened Redis socket gets bound to the first request's I/O context on CF Workers (`Cannot perform I/O on behalf of a different request`).
- This PR bypasses the singleton in the SIWE routes only — fresh `buildRedisClient(c.env)` per request, same pattern as `rate-limit-hono-cloudflare.ts` (which works fine in prod, confirmed live).
- Targeted hotfix to unblock agent → cloud SIWE wallet sign-in **today**. Follow-up PR replaces the singleton with a per-request `CacheClient` (ALS facade) and re-enables `CACHE_ENABLED=true` globally — at which point this bypass goes away.

## Why not just flip CACHE_ENABLED back on?
Because the singleton bug is real and would immediately re-break Steward sessions (the original 4h debug from yesterday). The proper fix is the follow-up; this PR just unblocks SIWE while keeping the singleton off.

## Why not call Steward's own `/auth/{nonce,verify}`?
Different contract — Steward returns a Steward JWT, not an `eliza_*` API key, and doesn't create the cloud user/org or grant initial credits. The agent skill (`packages/agent-skills/eliza-cloud/SKILL.md`) and SDK (`packages/sdk/src/public-routes.ts`) call `/api/auth/siwe/*` directly. Keeping the public contract intact.

## Changes
- `packages/lib/utils/siwe-helpers.ts`: `consumeNonce` and `validateAndConsumeSIWE` now take `redis: CompatibleRedis` as their first arg. New `issueNonce(redis)` helper allocates the random hex nonce and `SETEX`-stores it (replaces inline `randomHex` + `cache.set` in the route).
- `apps/api/auth/siwe/nonce/route.ts`: `buildRedisClient(c.env)` per request → 503 if no Redis bindings → `issueNonce(redis)`.
- `apps/api/auth/siwe/verify/route.ts`: same per-request client → passes `redis` into `validateAndConsumeSIWE`.

No other files touched. Singleton `cache` still imported by 53 other files which keep no-op'ing as before.

## Test plan
- [ ] `bun run typecheck` clean on the 3 touched files (verified locally — `grep -E "(siwe-helpers|siwe/nonce|siwe/verify)"` over typecheck output is empty).
- [ ] After deploying to staging: `curl https://api-staging.elizacloud.ai/api/auth/siwe/nonce?chainId=1` returns 200 with a valid nonce body.
- [ ] After deploying to staging: `bun run test:e2e:auth` passes (SIWE round-trip in `packages/tests/e2e/auth/siwe.test.ts` — currently tolerates 503, will go fully green).
- [ ] After deploying to prod: same `curl` against `api.elizacloud.ai`.
- [ ] Smoke: agent skill SIWE flow end-to-end.

## Risk
- Minimal. Per-request Redis is already the live pattern for rate-limiting in prod. Only the SIWE routes change; other code paths (Steward sessions, api-keys validation, etc.) are unaffected.
- Rollback: revert this commit; no schema or infra changes.
